title: Debate: ban private cars from the downtown core

items.text: Safety: far fewer traffic deaths and injuries, especially for pedestrians and cyclists
paraphrases: Safety: removing cars sharply cuts pedestrian injuries and deaths.
Fewer collisions and traffic fatalities downtown.
Streets become safe for children, older people and cyclists.

items.text: Public health: cleaner air and less noise in the densest part of the city
paraphrases: Cleaner air and less noise in the core.
Lower local exhaust pollution improves residents' respiratory health.
Public health gains from reduced air and noise pollution.

items.text: Economic vitality: more foot traffic, dwell time and spending; space for outdoor dining and events
paraphrases: Pedestrianized streets increase foot traffic and dwell time, which boosts spending.
Downtown vitality: outdoor dining, events and more people lingering.
Local businesses benefit from more walkers who stay longer.

items.text: Space efficiency: road and parking space is reallocated to people, transit lanes, green space or housing
paraphrases: Street and parking space can be reallocated to people, plazas and green space.
Cars use the most land per traveller; repurposing that space is efficient.
Parking lots could become housing or public realm.

items.text: Climate: lower emissions and a nudge toward low-carbon travel
paraphrases: Climate: cuts carbon emissions from short car trips.
Supports the city's greenhouse-gas reduction goals.
Encourages a shift to low-carbon modes.

items.text: Transit and mode shift: buses run faster and more reliably without car congestion, making transit and cycling more attractive
paraphrases: Buses get faster and more reliable once cars are out of the core.
Mode shift: walking, cycling and transit become more attractive.
Dedicated bus lanes increase ridership.

items.text: Business harm: shops and restaurants lose customers who drive, especially suburban shoppers, and may relocate to malls
paraphrases: Downtown shops and restaurants lose customers who arrive by car.
Retail revenue may decline as suburban shoppers go to malls instead.
Small businesses could suffer or relocate.

items.text: Accessibility: disabled and elderly people and others with limited mobility depend on door-to-door car access
paraphrases: People with disabilities and the elderly depend on door-to-door car access.
Accessibility for people with limited mobility suffers.
Wheelchair users and paratransit need exemptions.

items.text: Equity: people from areas with poor transit, shift workers and lower-income commuters lose access to downtown jobs and services
paraphrases: Equity: shift workers and lower-income commuters from areas with poor transit lose access to downtown jobs.
The ban is regressive for people who can't rely on transit.
Residents of outer neighborhoods bear the cost.

items.text: Displacement: traffic and parking pressure move to the surrounding neighborhoods and ring roads
paraphrases: Traffic is displaced onto surrounding neighborhoods and the ring road.
Spillover parking and congestion at the edge of the zone.
The ban pushes traffic elsewhere rather than eliminating it.

items.text: Logistics and services: deliveries, trades, emergency vehicles and residents' needs are harder to serve
paraphrases: Deliveries, freight and trades need vehicle access.
Emergency vehicles and service vehicles face complications.
Logistics for shops and residents get harder.

items.text: Transit readiness and implementation: without enough transit capacity first, access collapses; enforcement costs, political backlash
paraphrases: Transit capacity must exist first; otherwise people simply can't get downtown.
Implementation risk: enforcement costs and political backlash.
Premature ban before alternatives are ready.

cruxes.text: Are the alternatives (transit, cycling, park-and-ride, accessible options) good enough that people who drive now can still reach downtown?
paraphrases: Are transit and other alternatives good enough to replace car trips into the core?
Whether park-and-ride and bus capacity can substitute for driving.
Can people who currently drive still reach downtown by viable options?

cruxes.text: What is the net effect on downtown businesses and the local economy in this specific city (more walkers vs fewer drivers)?
paraphrases: Net economic effect: does gaining walkers outweigh losing drivers for downtown businesses?
Whether retail sales rise or fall after the ban is the empirical question.
The impact on the local economy depends on who currently shops downtown.

cruxes.text: Does car traffic disappear (mode shift / fewer trips) or just move to surrounding areas?
paraphrases: Does traffic evaporate or just get displaced onto nearby streets?
Whether trips disappear through mode shift or spill over to the surroundings.
Is it induced demand in reverse, or diversion?

cruxes.text: Values: how to weigh residents' and pedestrians' quality of life against access for people who drive in, and who bears the costs
paraphrases: Value question: how much to weigh residents' quality of life against access for commuters who drive.
Who bears the costs and who benefits - a distributional trade-off.
Whose downtown is it: people who live and walk there, or people who drive in?
